[h1][b] TLDR: Sells itself as an investigative puzzler but delivers a mostly on-rails visual novel experience. The handful of genuine puzzles are great, making their scarcity all the more frustrating.
[/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Neat investigative puzzles (ENHANCE….ENHANCE)
➕Some nice puzzles, like bomb defuse

[h1]NEUTRALS: [/h1]
🔹Story is good, but a bit too on-rails and hand-holding

[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Lots of unskippable intentionally blurry cutscenes leaves a cheap or vague feeling
➖Some reveals are not as big as they should be simply because you wouldn’t know things that your character would know

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely from a computer screen and is set in the 90s, we’re talking older CRT monitor screens. There’s not much exploration to be found, as you work for the government and everything is pretty locked down. I’d say the world is a bit basic and simple, only serving as a UI to show some puzzles. 

The narrative has some good parts. You play as Evan Tanner, a Federal Department of Investigation (FDI) operator, in which your job is to assist field agents. You very quickly learn that there’s something going on and you are enlisted, whether you want to or not, to uncover the truth. 
So while I did enjoy the story to an extent, any scene not at the computer and is told through a characters eyes is a blurry mess of objects that are nearly undecipherable. This could be something related to the story, but I don’t want to give the game the benefit of the doubt here and say that it worsens the experience. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The gameplay seems pretty cool at first, but you quickly realize how on-rails the game is. Essentially, this is a glorified visual novel with a few puzzles sprinkled in. At first, I felt like Garcia from Criminal Minds - I was the internet sleuth assisting agents in the field by giving them on-the-fly information to help with cases. But unfortunately, the game isn’t as cool as that. 
The loop consists of you having a conversation, being presented with evidence, and then using the 2-3 tools at your disposal to answer a question presented by the conversation. For example, you’ll need to identify a killer and a victim by scanning their faces to get their names, then look them up in the FDI database. Same thing with licenses plates or analyzing footage/pictures. It does sound very cool, but I can’t emphasize enough the on-rails experience and lack of deep puzzle mechanics. This is more of a game focused on the narrative. 

The difficulty is forgiving. I’m pretty sure I made every wrong choice in the game, yet still made it to the end. I literally messed up a [spoiler]bomb defuse and got an agent killed[/spoiler]. Whoops. Despite these consequences, this doesn’t seem like it impacted the game as much and wasn’t mentioned again other than a few brief times after the fact. 

[h1] [b] Graphics (Quality/Technical) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Being that the game is from the point of view of a computer screen and all “Real” scenes are a blurry mess, I’d say the quality isn’t great. What footage you do see is grainy 90’s-era quality, but aside from that the computer UI is good and crisp. 

On the technical side, I had no issues, encountered no bugs, and ran the game without issues. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The music isn’t really noticeable, but it does increase in intensity during high-drama parts. 

There is a lot of voice acting, and it all sounds good. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [2/10] [/b] [/h1]
Not a lot of replay value here, unless you want to redo the puzzles again for achievements. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The Operator is described as a game with detective/investigation, and puzzle elements. I’d estimate the game to be about 70% story/narrative focus, 20% puzzles, and 10% deducing or investigating. I’d say that Operator is an okay game, but I was a bit disappointed by the mystery and investigative sides. This is very much a visual novel game more than anything, and as someone that likes visual novels, I was expecting more to use my brain to make deductions instead of clicking pre-defined replies. 

The game does have a few puzzles. I’d say maybe ~10 at the most, and despite that small number, I found them to be good puzzles. Analyzing gunpowder was really cool. Defusing a bomb on the fly was also great. If the game was more focused on gameplay like that, then I’d give it a much higher score, but these are the highest highs that The Operator offers, and there’s only a few of them. 

The real focus of the game is on the narrative. While I wouldn’t consider the narrative to be bad, there were a few parts that were either ridiculously obvious, or a missed opportunity. 
Obvious, because of metagaming - anyone who watches mystery shows knows that there’s only so many characters who could be the culprit due to you the show introducing them to the viewer. Same concept here, it’s obviously going to be the handful of people you know about already. 
Missed opportunity because you as the player only know what you know. One part in particular [spoiler]has the player finding out his apartment is being watched with a camera, and you have to identify whose apartment it is[/spoiler]. Well how can you possibly figure that out without knowing anything about the characters' life, nor ever having been there? Dumb. 

Overall, I do recommend The Operator, but it’s important that you know what you’re going into. This is NOT about deduction or investigating, and that’s not necessarily a bad thing, but I feel the game presents itself in a way that it’s something that it isn’t. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
$14 base price is a bit much for a ~5 hour game with very low replay value. Wait for a sale. Around ~$5-7 would be a good point.

review_text_raw:
Played the demo and got really hooked, so I bought the game the next day full price.

AFTER the demo I expected it to be very similar to Orville and Cyber Manhunt, with the primary focus on using the game's mechanics to solve multiple criminal cases, most unrelated or maybe filler and some interconnected into a bigger picture.
It was... kinda like that? But instead of a focus on multiple cases and the solving mechanics, it focuses solely on one storyline.

Which to me was actually really sad I guess because the gameplay mechanics were really well implemented and would have made for a super nice gameplay loop but instead got used once to advance the plot and then got discarded (e.g. the lab analysis or manually unlocking files). 

Also, the game is probably 75% dialogue, in which you are given choices that lead nowhere. You feel like your choices should matter, maybe in resulting in different endings but there is only one ending implemented. It actually made me compare it more to a visual novel than a detective game.

The lack of "filler cases" is also more of a negative in this particular storyline. I've read that the developer wanted to focus more on the main story instead of filler but I think some filler would've helped the player to immerse themselves better into their role, made better usage of the well-implemented mechanics and would've allowed the player to connect with the characters better, settle mentally on the twists and turns of the main story and process them before the next thing gets thrown at them. It felt very fast-paced with no breathing time from basically the get-go and if I'm not mistaken the story takes place within only a couple of days in-game which also does not seem realistic.

Conclusion:
+ well-made from a technical point of view
+ well implemented mechanics
+ good soundtrack
- poor use of mechanics
- unclear advertisement (detective game vs. very story-driven, more of a visual novel)
- no actual choices made by the player even though it feels like they should have mattered
- lack of cases with a rather short gameplay time as a result
- lots of dialogue with comparatively little gameplay

If you're looking for somethin akin to Orville, Cyber Manhunt or even Her Story, this is not it.
I considered requesting a refund but I believe that if I buy a product, receive it and use it, there is no reason in refunding it, even if it was not what I expected

review_text_raw:
This game has so much going on that I would ideally like to praise but a lot of those same things are also why I didn't really enjoy it.  On the bright side it has a very clever user interface system I like where most of the game is controlled via a "computer", the puzzles range from really easy to more complicated, and the story has some creativity going on.  It's definitely somewhat interesting, very dialogue heavy, and I would not recommend if you're not a strong reader, lover of puzzle games, or if you like a lot of scenery or environment changes.

With that said, the user interface becomes tiring to interact with very quickly.  It's hard to convey a sense of importance or immediate action when most of the puzzles really come down to clicking and having a computer "analyze" random clues.  The puzzles don't scale well in difficulty nor do they feel like they have a good payoff - any skill you learn will either be used again and again because we have to have some way to drive the game or it's a one time use - why did we bother to spend so much time reworking the wheel for no reason? (Example slight spoiler: you will never need to analyze anything other than the one sample in the game).  The instructions are lacking a lot - they have a help button that is definitely useful but there's an element of figure it out here that at times seems un-necessary.  I really don't understand not sticking to more tried and true puzzle formats particularly because they would have felt more rewarding, helped the game, and surely been easier to execute with more precision.

The story is the last complaint I'm going to throw out there.  It's interesting and I want to be invested, however, it is rushed, let down by a lot of bad music and sound interaction, and I found myself uninvested in the characters including my own character frequently.  Any story is going to ask you to slightly engage in disbelief but if you're an analytical or practical thinker there is going to come a point where you realize this is almost like a bad tv fiction.  If you're ever watched a non believable show you enjoyed - something like bones comes to mind - this is taking the worse parts of we can rush a story, analysis, evidence, data, blah blah blah but without any of the charm of why it matters.

Interesting idea but a bit of a miss on execution for me and kind of a feeling of  . . .  why did I spend time on this? lol.

review_text_raw:
I recommend it ... but with some qualifications. 

So, the presentation is excellent. Really builds a strong atmosphere of mystery. There are points when you really feel like you're an operator for a field agent uncovering a major conspiracy. The game does a very good job of doing that. Some of the puzzles took some thinking. They're not super-difficult, but they all make sense in the context of the game and there's not a lot of handholding. Overall, I like how it's all presented.

However ... what I didn't realize is that this is more visual novel than a true puzzle game. It's not a pure visual novel - there is some genuine gameplay here. And that gameplay is pretty good. But ultimately, the gameplay is to trigger the next scene. You can't really "fail" - or at least, you can't fail in a way that will affect the story.

I had believed the game to be a puzzler in the vein of Obra Dinn or Orwell. And I would say the gameplay is as good in part. But after a while, I could "see the rails" - see that at its core, it's a visual novel.

However, that's not why I was disappointed.

The bigger problem I had with the game is that I felt it was ... too short. Not in terms of game length - but in terms of the plot. It felt like it ended right when the plot was getting interesting. 

Putting spoilers on anything further:
[spoiler]Where the game ends, when the intrigue is getting intense and the identity twist is revealed ... I felt almost like that's where the real story is starting. 

Up until this point, our protagonist has just been faceless tech guy who doesn't have a role in the story - and suddenly now we understand how he ties into the conspiracy. And we also understand just what kind of terrible enemy we're up against. 

With this dramatic twist, we now understand the protagonist and his role in the story - as well as true nature and threat of the antagonist that he faces. The stakes have been made clear. The die is cast, the point of no return is reached. 

The question is, what happens now? What does our protagonist do with his new forbidden knowledge? And how can he defeat this terrible enemy?... but instead - the story unceremoniously ends right there. Not only is it kind of a bummer of an ending - but it feels like you stopped telling me this story exactly at the point where it became interesting. Right at the point where things had fully shifted from "Government Bureau Employee Simulator" to "Global Spy Conspiracy Thriller". Our agency has revealed they're evil and they betrayed us, we're gonna go rogue, and take the conspiracy down .... no, wait, actually, that's the end. [/spoiler] 
 
[spoiler]It'd be like if moments after Jason Bourne realized that he was a secret agent and that assassins were trying to kill him ... he just died and the movie ended.

Or, to use a videogame equivalent - it'd be like if right when it's revealed that Doki Doki Literature Club is not actually an anime dating sim ... the game just ended.

There's no resolution. The story feels incomplete. If anything, this feels like it should be the prologue to the real plot. Like a teaser that gives us a glimpse of "OMG these guys are really bad". 

Actually, at the end, when it shifts to HAL's perspective - I thought that was where the real game was about to begin. like, "Twist, Tanner dies in the prologue! You're actually playing as HAL. How will HAL defeat the Organization?" ... But then the credits rolled.[/spoiler] 
 
[spoiler]Part of the problem was that I figured out the twist long before it was revealed. I wasn't being clever, either - it was clear from the opening cutscene that we were not playing as some anonymous rando. We are obviously someone who is involved with this conspiracy in some way. As events played out, the only possibilities were either (a) you were secretly one of the missing people or (b) you were secretly the Ghost. When it became clear you weren't the Ghost ... well, there's only one missing person who we know by name, so that must be you.[/spoiler] 
 
I will say I was thoroughly engaged up until the ending. Even when it started to become clear that the story was more on rails that I'd hoped - I didn't mind because the presentation was so good and the story had me hooked. 

But when it ended ... I felt very disappointed because I was like, "Wait, we're ending it here? That's it?"

So I guess that's my recommend. It's a very well-done experience and the devs clearly were doing something right to keep me gripped. I intended to just try the game for a bit and ended up finishing it in one setting. But it really surprised me that it ended where it did.

I would prefer to give this game a 5/10, but unfortunately, that's not possible on Steam, so I’m rating it negatively for interested buyers to see.

I bought the game to unravel mysteries as an FBI operative—a game I could play for several hours. The gameplay mechanics are exactly what I was hoping for, but unfortunately, some of them are only used once throughout the entire game.
The story is extremely short, with a plot that becomes obvious within the first 40 minutes of gameplay. Seriously, 2 hours of gameplay for 14€? Not to meantion an "Original Soundtrack" for another 10€. If players could skip some dialogues and cutscenes, the game would only last 30 minutes. The story feels more like a detective TV show where everything is "weird," "doesn't make sense," and "everything is interconnected."

In summary:
+ The game mechanics are awesome! - Unfortunately, their potential is wasted on a simplistic story with a soap-opera-like plot seen more than thousands of times on TV.
+ The soundtrack (not bought), sound effects, and voice acting are excellent.
- The story is simple and feels rather sloppy (95% of the ideas went into coding and mechanics, 5% into the story). Perhaps it's due to the potential for a speedrunning community?
- When I calculate the "price per hour" of the main story, this game is undoubtedly the worst in my entire game library (7€ per hour (almost 12€ if you buy the "original soundtrack"), including cutscenes and dialogues).
- The game has unskippable cutscenes (returning home), dialogues (the tutorial), and end credits, likely so that you can’t get a refund within the 2-hour Steam policy.
? If the sequel to this game will also be only 2 hours long, the developers might as well not even bother. It’s not worth the money.

If the game was a bit longer (at least 4 hours of a decent story), I would recommend it, but unfortunately, I can't.
Definitely buy it during a sale, just not now.

review_text_raw:
This game only has one ending, and only less than 2½ - 3 hours of content in total, making the cost per played hour very high. 
The one singular ending is quite bad, and even though there are many dialogue options, there are no actual meaningful choices to be made.
There are numerous quite long and somewhat boring unskippable cut scenes. However one could argue that having no skip option is acceptable due to it being somewhat important to pay attention to the them. And since there's only one ending, there's no replayability, and so there's no need to have a skip option. Though realistically, and as others have pointed out, the most probable reason for not having a skip option is to extend the required playtime to over 2 hours so the game cannot be refunded through Steam.
The game has a lot of dialogue, and not a lot of gameplay. What little actual gameplay there is, is enjoyable enough I guess, but also pretty simplistic and easy. This can be seen as both a positive and a negative. If you're looking for any sort of a challenge/puzzle, you will not find it in this game. This game should be definitely thought of as a visual novel more than a puzzle game.
The story itself is mediocre and actually pretty shallow, which is very bad for a game that consists mainly of the story.
The dialogue is fully voice-acted (except for [spoiler]HAL[/spoiler] and the protagonist), which is a definite plus. The voice acting is also pretty high-quality. However I cannot help but feel like way too much developer effort and money was put into the voice acting, when it should've been put into other aspects of the game.
The soundscape and the soundtrack are also good, but really nothing out of the ordinary.

Overall, The Operator is a short, pricey mediocre dialogue-heavy and minimal-gameplay game with high-quality voice acting and heavy hand-holding and railroading, and with only one ending. It feels like the game was designed to be just long enough to make it impossible to refund after reaching the ending (which in fairness one shouldn't do regardless, if they enjoyed the game and reached the ending).

I cannot recommend anything else but to watch someone else such as a YouTuber play this game. I think that will actually add way more to the experience than buying the game and playing it on your own.

review_text_raw:
Some interesting concepts and a fun story. Cool twist too. Most of the puzzles were relatively straightforward, but the "manual reading" one was actually pretty exciting and interesting, and the "identifying the feed" one was clever. I just could not get past the ridiculous anachronisms popping up constantly, and some very confusing internal logic.

This game takes place in 1992. Everybody has a cell phone, digital photography is commonly accessible, "zoom, enhance" is an actual mechanic. The game's FBI analogue has a database with facial recognition data of nearly everyone in the country? In 1992??? In 2025 sure, but not in 1992. Agents are constantly uploading files to your computer from their phone. At one point, confusingly, an agent apparently sends you physical floppy disks.... via his phone...? Baffling honestly. I was willing to set aside the fact that VoIP didn't exist in 1992 either, but after a while you simply cannot suspend your disbelief any further. 

HAL's "hacking" capabilities are completely inconsistent, and the justifications for why they can't hack a particular thing make no narrative sense a lot of the time. Credit where credit's due though, nothing stands out to me as anachronistic about HAL's methods at least.

There's a big narrative-UX disconnect as well. Initially I thought the "phone calls" you receive from agents are just game objects showing transcripts of audio conversations, but at one point you're instructed to *enter a code into the chat box* as though it were a terminal. So now I'm asked to believe that my computer has been *actually transcribing* phone calls automatically while people are speaking to me, and that I can use this function as a terminal. Completely ridiculous. 

This game would have made way more sense if it were set in the current year, with minimal changes to the story or mechanics, but I think the devs were just too enamoured with the retro aesthetic to let it go so they set it in the 90s anyways. 

Side note: I had annoying bug where my keybinds weren't showing up in-game, so anything where I was required to press a key just had [???] instead. Not game breaking, just annoying.

review_text_raw:
Aesthetically pleasing, good story with at the very least, decent voice acting if not great. Runs well. An interesting gameplay mechanic that has you sitting at your desk, putting together pieces of the puzzles as agents sweep the field for evidence and follow the leads you help develop. The story has you unraveling a conspiracy, using computer tools, metadata, and analyzing software to pull the narrative together. It's fascinating, and the game does a really good job at making you feel like you're truly a professional analyst, solving crimes from the comfort of a desk in Washington DC.

Problem is, the game is pretty darn short. Only about 4 hours of gameplay, and it feels deeply on rails, to the point that the puzzle portion of it feels more like a addon to the rest of the game. If you subscribe to the $1 per hour mindset, even discounted to $9, this game is technically not worth it, as the game has limited replayability. Though, the game does make up for it with the story and gameplay to a degree. It is, at the very least, a pretty impactful 4 hours, and you could get somewhat different results if you repeat the story, so there is a small sense that your choices matter. 

I might just be spoiled, coming off of The Roottrees are Dead which had a fairly similar premise of using a computer to uncover information that can fill in the blanks. But in TRaD, they introduce you to the tools and then you spend a bulk of the time using them on your own to fill in profiles on the family tree. There was a lot more blanks to fill in and time to spend fiddling around with information. With TO, you get introduced to cool mechanics and tools on your computer, and then use almost none of them ever again. The game feels like a 4 hour tutorial other than the story, which takes interesting turns and, as a flipside, keeps the player continously faced with new and interesting problems to solve. It sucks not being able to repeatedly use a mechanic I got familiar with or a handbook I just learned, but every in-game day pulls me straight in with a curveball, gameplay wise or story wise.

The ending kinda left a bad taste in my mouth. AFAIK, your choices don't really seem to affect the ending from what I saw online in guides and gameplay.

Still gonna leave it as a positive review, because I quite enjoyed this and I think the devs are absolutely cooking here. I just hope the developers consider putting more meat on the bones of TO2, because it feels like there is a ton of potential for a truly great puzzle/detective game here that only gets partially realized.

review_text_raw:
I don't think this game is quite what I expected. It's a style of game I'd love to see more of. But while I still mostly enjoyed my time with it, I'm left wanting more.

The story itself is interesting and has enough of those classic thriller movie twist and turns to keep you engaged throughout. Role-playing the "man in the chair" is pretty fun, and you have a few moments that deliver on that promise, at least from a narrative standpoint.

After playing this through once, you'd think the game had multiple endings. You are left wondering if maybe there's some way to correct your mistakes and change the outcome. That is not the case. The ending is pretty bleak, comes pretty quickly (the game itself only being a few hours long at most), and doesn't bring the story to a proper close. I can do without a "good ending", but there's a disappointing lack of closure here.

Broadly speaking, The Operator fails to deliver on the use of "detective skills" it says you'll need in the game's description. You definitely interact with a computer and run a few faux-terminal commands, but most of the time you're just finding a name or a face by clicking the a button that Zoom-Enhances a video CSI style. It sure looks like you're doing the work, but none of it is very challenging and it all feels a little superficial.

There's maybe one section that raises the difficulty and that's because it puts you on a timer and forces you to read an instruction manual. It's the first and only challenging moment the game offers. It was actually a pretty good moment, and the game could have done with a few more scenes this.

I'd not recommend this game to fans of puzzle games who are looking for a challenge, but it's still a fun journey if you want to spend a few hours in the world of a thriller movie. Just don't expect a satisfying ending.

review_text_raw:
This is an excellent, short puzzle and story game as an Operator in the FDI assisting agents with cases

The game opens with a cut scene which you watch and this sets the tone. Then you see a computer terminal boot up and you log in. This is the start of your job as an operator for the FDI (Federal Department of Intelligence). This is the main screen you see and involves taking calls, running through evidence and assisting agents with their cases.

There is a small cast of characters – you assist a few agents, you hear from the director, who is a friend, and you have a direct supervisor. There are also a couple of other people you hear from. To start with the calls walk you through the basics of the set up and the mechanics you will be using. Then you are given your first call from an agent.

The element of “assisting” agents is fun and about solving puzzles. Finding people in databases, working out how to get evidence from clues in video and audio files and some careful reading of instructions and asking questions. I found the puzzles varied, fun, hard (but not too hard) and appropriate to the setting. The difficulty curve generally increases as the game progresses.

The other people are interesting and I generally liked them, particularly the agents. They were varied, plausible and interesting. There were a couple of dialogue choices where I would have not chosen from the options given, but mostly they were plausible too.

The progression of the different cases builds the stories, tone and difficulty of the puzzles. Also, the puzzles generally get harder, although one or two of the later ones are still quite quick.

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 98:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆☆ (8/10)

[i] The Operator [/i] casts you not as a hero in the field, but as the analyst—the voice behind the computer—supporting agents from the shadows. It’s a fascinating setup and a fresh twist on crime-solving games, and usually almost always lives up to its potential!

🖥[b] Pros: [/b]
[list]
[*] Authentic "operator" fantasy. You monitor missions from your desk, field phone calls, look through mysterious documents, and scrub through CCTV footage. 

[*] Diverse tools. The game gives you a chem scanner, facial recognition database, image enhancement tech, and document search systems. For example, in one mission, you identify a suspect by cross-referencing a blurry security camera with an equally blurry security footage of his car and license plate. That kind of detective work feels cool. You feel smart when it works.

[*] Great use of puzzles under pressure. A standout moment has you guiding a field agent through bomb defusal. You have to analyze chemicals, check your reference files, and read out step-by-step instructions—all while the timer ticks down. These time-sensitive missions are where the game shines.

[*] Well-done audio design. The UI clicks, radio static, and phone calls all contribute to a grounded, late-'90s thriller vibe. The voice acting is low-key but sells the scenario well, especially during moments of stress or confusion.

[*] No filler. It’s tight and focused. No wandering, no padding. You’re thrown into the action quickly and missions move at a brisk pace.
[/list]

[b]🧾 Cons: [/b]
[list]
[*] Flat characters. The field agents and mysterious hacker HAL are more archetypes than flesh-and-blood. They push the story forward, but rarely surprise

[*] Choices don’t matter much. There are dialogue branches, but most are cosmetic. Whether you’re professional or snarky, or even whether you succeed or fail at certain puzzles, the game mostly funnels you into the same story beats.

[*] Abrupt ending. The game ends just as things get interesting. HAL’s storyline ramps up, then vanishes. You barely get to dig into the conspiracy or see the consequences of your actions. It feels like a miniseries that ends on episode three.
[/list]

I would classify this as a short narrative game with very light puzzles.

PUZZLES
A majority of the puzzles are signposted and obvious, and they all give a tutorial vibe. The game will teach you how to solve a particular type of puzzle, but then that type of puzzle is never visited again.

There were two puzzles that weren't, but these felt frustrating as:
- the first one had VERY confusing wording and used terms that were not explained ("tickable" being the word I got stuck on)
- the second one you needed to brute force a solution, which is never fun nor rewarding

NARRATIVE
For a mystery game, the final twist was basically shouted at the beginning of the game and I guessed it within the first 5 minutes. All of the cases pertain to the main mystery (no side missions to divert your attention). When you know the secret right away, it's hard to feel motivated to continue playing.

In the end, I felt it was a shallow, predictable, and simple game. It has good bones, but needed a lot more time in the oven

If a sequel does come along, or this team makes a similar game, I hope they:
- Include more puzzles
- Not make the ending obvious
- Playtest all the puzzles to make sure that things are easily understood and enjoyable (without losing the theme)
- Add in some red herrings/busywork 
- Show off their systems! Similar to a Hypnospace Outlaw or The Roottrees are Dead, have us use the mechanics more than once before moving on to a completely different thing. I would have loved to do more searching, scrubbing, etc in the game but didn't have enough opportunities outside each mechanic's single puzzle.

This is a pretty solid game, at least the first time around. I've only been through it once, but I am curious about how it will be after a few runs. It's definitely a bit shorter than I thought (this run was around 3 hours), and while I didn't do much research on it before buying it (other than reading the tags and brief parts of the description), it seemed a bit different than what I expected. I was kind of thinking you'd go through and help solve multiple cases, and just keep going that way with increasing difficulty and depth as you continue playing. It's not that. It sort of starts that way, but doesn't stay that way for long. It's VERY linear as far as I can tell, and while I think there are different outcomes based on player inputs, I have yet to try that. It's not the investigation game it's labeled as. It's still well put together and thought out, but I felt a little bit misled, as there is really only one single "case" that you're working on as the player, it just happens to include a few other cases that you work on in the tutorial stages. 

Without spoiling it, I think it's a good game, though I don't know if I would pay full price for it. I think if you could get it for under $10 USD it would be a much better value, personally. But, we'll see how it goes on the replay-ability of the game and that might change. I'm curious how different actions and responses affect the outcome of the game for sure. 

Soundtrack really buffed this game a lot too, it was really well timed and well orchestrated. 

My main complaint is some of the cutscenes are ridiculously long for what their substance is. There is basically no substance to most of them, it's just some sound effects and maybe the occasional spot of dialogue.

As someone else said in their review, it scratched an itch I didn't know I had, but I would've been much more excited to see some real investigating. Like phasmophobia, but you're the computer geek at this government intelligence agency. If you play through the first hour or so, you'll see sort of what I mean by that.

review_text_raw:
The Operator is a very short (3 to 4 hours at best) interactive visual novel with good production value. The interface looks clean and easy to use, the voice acting is good, and the interactive elements are pretty decent. For a visual novel. 

It is presented, however, as a game of deduction and puzzle solving. The puzzles and deductions are shallow with too much handholding. As you progress new mechanics are introduced, and then discarded immediately after. This gives the mistaken impression that much more content is waiting for you and puzzles will get more difficult. And then the game is over.

The story is equally shallow. The opening scene reveals too much, making the big reveal at the end something you can piece together within a few minutes of playing the game. The ending is a cliffhanger of sorts, but it makes this game feel like the opening chapter of a larger story that has not been written. Worse is that none of the conspiracy is ever explained, leaving you with many questions that are unlikely to be answered. There are no divergent paths, only one ending, and zero replay value.

If you go into this game expecting a visual novel, you will have an entertaining few hours with an okay story and underwhelming finale. If you go into this game expecting deduction, investigation, and puzzle solving, you will find only disappointment. This ultimately leads to my negative review. For a visual novel it is too short with an unresolved story, and for an investigation game the puzzles are too simple. The Operator has a lot of unmet potential, which is a shame.

Overall enjoyable. Decent interface and storyline, good variety of puzzle mechanics, low to medium difficulty and complexity.

I'm usually not a fan of dialogue choices and multiple endings, so I didn't know how to feel when I found out this game [i]doesn't[/i] have alternative endings.  Like another user put it, it really felt like I had reached the "bad ending", and that I was supposed to make different choices.  But playing through a second time did not change the outcomes aside from slightly different dialogue, and seeing one or two subtle hints I had missed the first time around.

And the developer has confirmed that it's not intended to be replayable (see the dev's [url=https://steamcommunity.com/app/1771980/discussions/0/4511002214535949429/]community post[/url])

The interface is quite well done, with a variety of technical mechanics.  The in-game documents and user manuals are quite impressively believable in style, while staying relevant to the gameplay, and to the storyline.  I quite enjoyed the [spoiler]"Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes"[/spoiler] style puzzle.

I was a little disappointed that the terminal was so limited, but given this is a relatively small game, that's understandable.

At times, especially at the start, it felt like a bit of information overwhelm moving too quickly, but it generally seems to be quite forgiving (though I haven't tested what happens if you don't answer a call, or fail to [spoiler]defuse the bomb[/spoiler]).

Often it felt a bit too heavy on the handholding.  [spoiler]The "watch me."  "Are you watching me?" prompts for the scripted surveillance made me giggle[/spoiler].  Most of the big reveals were heavily hinted at early on so I knew long before the characters themselves knew.  There were a couple that surprised me though.

The voice acting was quite good.  As was the sound design, and animations.  There's quite a few unskippable animations but they're generally done quite well and relevant to the storyline or puzzles.

Overall decent little game.  First playthrough took me just about under ~6hrs at a meandering pace (and not keeping track of breaks).  Would play a sequel if it's ever made.

review_text_raw:
I'm pretty conflicted regarding my thoughts on this game, if there was a neutral review that would be my rating. 

On one hand the game is very polished, especially for an indie game. It's OST really sets the mood and switches at the perfect time to give you goosebumps. The mechanics are pretty fleshed out; providing a decent challenge while also not being so hard that would require one to search up guides on them. The story is also really thought out and you will get invested into it very quick.

The unfortunate problem I have with this game is that it's extremely short. You can tell by the average 3 hour playtime in the reviews. Additionally all the content + mechanics that the game will throw at your are pretty much in the trailer. (There's only like 10 cases in total) Additionally, all game choices seems to not divert things from the main ending, which means that the game is not very re-playable. There may be some secrets as hinted by the credits achievement or that can be activated by a certain specific sequence of events, but they aren't readily accessible and would require probably some video tutorial guide.

And that leads to the big question, should you buy the game? I honestly can't say in good faith that it is worth it to buy the listed price ($14 USD). If you have a good amount of spare money to spend on games, then go for it. But for most people, I'd recommend holding out on purchasing the game unless it has a heavy sale.

I would not say the game is worth full price to be honest maybe on a deep discount. Only buy if you are looking for an interactive story more than a detective/puzzle game.

It's an ok game to kill a couple hours. I'm recommending, because I love that people make these kind of games, but I am a bit disappointed. It's VERY easy. The demo gave me Vigil Cases vibe, but turned out the game has incredibly strong and inescapable hand-holding. It's like Vigil Cases in tutorial mode. I thought I'd be looking through a bunch of databases and burrowing into various documents to find details that would solve cases. In reality I was mostly clicking on the dialogue, where NPCs would tell me exactly what to do, which usually involved no more than opening one file, looking up one name, or following a list of instructions.

There was a lot of lost potential here. Like, there's literally zero point in the terminal: the player never gets to figure out what command they should enter, it's always provided by the NPCs. There's no choice who to call, or what information to tell them, except in a couple places. I counted two cool puzzles that gave you an "Aha" moment, the rest was unfortunately easy and predictable.

In short, if you're looking for something to scratch the 'Golden Idol" or "Roottrees are Dead" itch, I wouldn't get your hopes up.

The game markets itself as a mystery and conspiracy genre piece which it lives up to. It is very text-based in the vein of Hacknet where you're attached to a computer terminal for the entirety of the game (voice acting present though). Outside of one really great and tense sequence it's mostly clicking through simple instructions and doing some deductions to progress. It's interesting and compelling but the playtime is lacking to fully explore the concept. The store description mentions working on many cases and assisting agents but everything done is very attached to the central story where some more diversity in content of the cases would be appreciated to pad out the fantasy of doing the detective work and better utilize the mechanics introduced. I wish it was easier to play though certain sections of the game to make different choices without playing through the whole game again.

I would recommend this game on sale but at full price, it's too quick to finish to enjoy completely.

[spoiler]Mystery is actually kind of predictable and because there's so much to do with the main story, everything is obviously a hint for the ending twist. Like Arkham Knight, it's easy to guess the twists before they happen which mutes the impact of those moments.[/spoiler]

review_text_raw: The concept of the operator is super interesting. But unfortunately there's not a lot to explore and investigate here. We're constantly guided by other characters and told the very thing we need to find, one thing after the next. It's like the game never gets past the tutorial, and it never gets to the point where you get to do more advanced research. This simple game mechanic is not super satisfying. It feels more like a short story turned into a game than a real detective game. It's on a very different level compared to other detective games such as Return of the Obra Dinn, The Roottrees are Dead or The Case of the Golden Idol. It's also very short, I finished it in less than 4 hours and there's no replayability. Also be very careful with the saves, there are save points and you'll lose progress if you don't quit at exactly the right times. On the plus side, the interface is quite well done and the voices are nice (though I'm not sure why it makes my computer boiling hot when the graphics are so simple). I liked the bomb defusing part the most, and it's a shame we can't replay that part again.

review_text_raw:
The Operator is a really fun, if unbearably short, adventure game that scratches the itch I've had since playing Hypnospace Outlaw. Cyber-sleuthing to solve and aid crimes and slowly diving into a conspiracy? What's not to like?

I wish it was a bit longer or the main plot was a bit drawn out, however. The game starts you off with a simple tutorial, but it drops you immediately into a fullfledged conspiracy that's the driving force of the entire game. Some little bit of fluff would have been nice. Analyze a video to solve an armed robbery, cross-reference tattoos to uncover gang affiliations, find out a victim's next of kin to get more information, or even just zoom in an ID what home a missing cat belongs to. There's endless possibilities for this kind of concept that are just underutilized. It left me wanting more when the reality was I only had a limited set of things to do.

The game is still exceptionally well made and the soundtrack keeps you engaged through all the twists and reveals, even if they were obvious in the first place. It's a good afternoon game.

Got this game, played it. Felt mixed at the end.
Pros:
- It's a pretty good on a technical level. It's a reasonably accurate portrayal of someone working security, albeit with some obvious creative liberties taken.
- The music was great

Cons:
- It's shorter than you'd think
- There are some parts that were confusing.
- The hints felt like you were being talked down to.

Compare and contrast with, say, The Root Trees are Dead, which is a bit different, but it has similar detective vibes. RTaD felt like you were peeling back layers of an onion to find the secrets buried in a mountain of info. The Operator felt like you were in an onion peeling factory that had you operate cool machines, but treated like you were dumb for not knowing which nob made middle onion layers go off.

I didn't want to hit the thumbs down this because it is worth your time, but maybe not $10 worth of time.

Compare and contrast with, say, The Root Trees are Dead, which is a bit different, but it has similar detective vibes. RTaD felt like you were peeling back layers of an onion to find the secrets buried in a mountain of info. The Operator felt like you were in an onion peeling factory that had you operate cool machines, but treated like you were dumb for not knowing which nob made middle onion layers go off. I didn't want to hit the thumbs down this because it is worth your time, but maybe not $10 worth of time.

review_text_raw:
The only thing puzzling about “The Operator” is why it has so many positive reviews. It’s too simple to deserve the “Investigation” or “Detective” tags. At heart, it’s an atmospheric, highly polished point-and-click adventure, closer to a children’s interactive TV show than an actual investigation puzzle game.

It gets slightly interesting during the [spoiler]bomb-defusing segment[/spoiler], but, like everything else in this game, that’s just an exercise in following instructions rather than piecing together clues. Nothing in this game justifies the admission price, don't recommend.

review_text_raw:
A pretty good, pretty short mystery game.  Difficulty level is fairly low, though it still manages to make you feel clever by laying off with the hand-holding early on; that's a good design decision that seems rare in this genre.

The story is intriguing and engaging, with solid voice acting, but just when it seems like it's about to get really good, it ends... What seems intended to have been the Big Twist of the entire thing, is something which I had already guessed (spoiler for [i]when[/i] you start seeing info relevant to the big reveal: [spoiler]in the very first case[/spoiler]), and anyone who spends a moment contemplating the overarching story will probably come to the same conclusion, long before the "big reveal" and its hammy sound effects.

Still, it was brief and enjoyable.  I don't see too many games in this genre, and this one is slightly above average.  I would look forward to playing a sequel.

review_text_raw:
This was a really fun story based game! I'd describe it as the most interactive visual novel I've ever played--You're not doing more than point/clicking through the story and it's never unclear what you're supposed to be looking for/interacting with, so mostly you're experiencing the story as if you were that particular character. The immersion was typically pretty deep, especially if you're playing on your PC as that's what the character is actually doing in the story, so it's very easy to put yourself into their shoes and get taken along for the ride. 

I was pleasantly surprised at how it shifted from you being a pretty backseat part of the investigation to having a very active role. If it feels a little too easy in the beginning but you're intrigued by the story, stick around and enjoy the ride!
